seo.meta_title: Yes or No to Negative Questions in Korean | '아직 안 끝났어?'
seo.meta_description: Why Koreans answer '응' to 'You're not done yet?' when they aren't done. How 네 and 아니요 work with negative questions, and why AI gets it backwards.

ai_failure.situation: A friend checks in on your assignment: '아직 안 끝났어?' (You're not done yet?) You aren't done, and want to say 'No, not yet.'
ai_failure.ai_mistake: Follows English logic: 'No, not yet' becomes '아니, 아직 안 끝났어.' and 'Yes, I'm done' becomes '응, 끝났어.'
ai_failure.why_it_fails: Korean 응/네 and 아니/아니요 answer whether the question is right, not whether the fact is positive. Starting with 아니 tells the listener 'you're wrong', so they may think you've finished — then the rest of your sentence says the opposite.

natural_solution.rule: With a negative question, agree or disagree with the question itself. If it's true (you're not done), start with 응/네. If it's wrong (you are done), start with 아니/아니요. When unsure, skip yes/no and just state the fact.

alternatives.context: You're still not done — agreeing with '아직 안 끝났어?'
You've actually finished — disagreeing with the question
Polite reply to '아직 식사 안 하셨어요?' (Haven't you eaten yet?) when you haven't

nuance: English yes and no follow the fact: if you're not done, you say 'no' whatever the question was. Korean 네 and 아니요 work more like 'Right' and 'That's not right' — they respond to the speaker's sentence. So when someone asks a negative question (아직 안 끝났어?, 안 매워요?, 내일 안 와요?), agreeing that the negative is true means saying 네/응. This trips up learners in both directions, and a mismatch can lead to real misunderstandings: a manager who hears '아니요' to '보고서 아직 안 보냈어요?' (You haven't sent the report yet?) will assume it has been sent. The safest habit is to follow 네 or 아니요 with the full verb, so the meaning survives even if the first word lands wrong: 네, 아직 안 보냈어요 / 아니요, 아까 보냈어요.
